query: Earlier studies used carbothermal shock, fast moving-bed pyrolysis, microwave heating, polyol synthesis, and dealloying, but a straightforward, cost-effective, and scalable route remains unavailable. Prior comparative work produced sharply different outcomes among multimetal nanoparticle systems—including homogeneous alloy formation versus phase separation, elemental segregation, uncontrolled morphology, and high decomposition temperatures—without establishing a general cause. The challenge increases with more than five interacting elements and the requirement to preserve substantial surface-atom exposure for catalytic applications. Against this background, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis explains what governs successful formation of noble metal–based high-entropy alloy nanoparticles and why? Describe one controlled comparison without naming the variable or investigative technique, predict the observations relative to an unchanged baseline, define where the hypothesis should and should not apply, relate it to the reported comparative evidence, and identify a decisive falsifying result.

generation.hypothesis: The key to forming homogeneous noble metal–based HEA nanoparticles is that a rapid, nearly simultaneous decomposition of the mixed metal precursors kinetically traps the high‐entropy state. By minimizing atomic diffusion during nucleation, the synthesis process 'freezes' the alloy before atoms can segregate, thus preventing phase separation.
generation.material_initial_state: A uniform, co‐crystallized or well‐mixed single-source precursor composed of noble metal salts or complexes.
generation.intervention: Implement a synthesis process with an ultrafast thermal treatment (e.g., fast moving bed pyrolysis or carbothermal shock) compared to a slower, conventional heating protocol.
generation.conditions: Applicable under rapid heating/cooling regimes at relatively low temperatures (compared to high-temperature equilibrium synthesis) where atomic mobility is suppressed, particularly for noble metal–based systems prepared from single-source precursors.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of numerous small nuclei under high supersaturation conditions that, due to limited atomic mobility, preserve the random elemental distribution.
generation.mechanism: The rapid thermal pulse drives a simultaneous decomposition of all precursor species, which results in a burst nucleation event. The ensuing high nucleation density combined with an ultrafast cooldown prevents significant atomic diffusion, thereby kinetically locking in the mixed elemental configuration and forestalling phase separation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to slower heating, the rapid synthesis yields nanoparticles with a uniform, single-phase alloy structure and homogeneous elemental distribution, while the slower process leads to phase-segregated or compositionally inhomogeneous particles.
generation.baseline: Nanoparticles produced via conventional, slower thermal treatment that allow sufficient time for differential reduction and subsequent atomic diffusion, resulting in phase or elemental segregation.
generation.boundary: This mechanism should hold in systems where the thermal pulse is fast enough to outpace atomic diffusion and where the precursor chemistry allows uniform decomposition. It is not expected to apply in high-temperature equilibrium synthesis or in systems with intrinsically high atomic mobilities that overcome kinetic trapping.
generation.uncertainty: The precise kinetic thresholds (e.g., critical heating/cooling rates) and the dependence on specific precursor chemistries remain to be quantitatively defined.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two sets of noble metal HEA nanoparticles using identical precursor mixtures but different thermal protocols: one with an ultrafast heating/cooling cycle and one with a significantly slower thermal ramp. Characterize the elemental distribution and phase purity of the nanoparticles using high-resolution imaging and diffraction techniques.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the ultrafast thermal treatment does not result in a higher degree of homogeneous, single-phase alloy formation (i.e., if no significant improvement in elemental mixing is observed or if phase segregation is similar to or worse than the slow treatment), then the hypothesis that kinetic trapping via rapid processing governs HEA nanoparticle formation would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Bulk materials have very low dispersion, i.e., a low ratio of surface to bulk atoms. A large surface-to-bulk atom ratio is, however, vital for efficient catalysts. Nanoparticles possess such high dispersion. This generates a large interest in developing HEA nanoparticle synthesis methods. Many synthesis methods for HEA nanoparticles are high-energy shock methods such as Joule-heating, microwave heating, laser-ablation, and fast-bed pyrolysis. Recent studies propose that it is also possible to use low-temperature solution-based techniques to synthesize HEA nanoparticles or low-temperature reduction of solid precursors. Such methods open for fine-tuning both the composition and nanostructure of nanoparticles. For high-temperature synthesis approaches, entropy plays a role in stabilizing the multi-metallic phases, so that single-phase materials can be prepared. Thermal shock methods are also believed to freeze the material in a state of high entropy during controlled cool-down. High-entropy alloy (HEA) nanoparticles (NPs) exhibit unusual combinations of functional properties. However, their scalable synthesis remains a significant challenge requiring extreme fabrication conditions. Metal salts are often employed as precursors because of their low decomposition temperatures, yet contain potential impurities. Here, we propose an ultrafast (< 100 ms), one-step method that enables the continuous synthesis of HEA NPs directly from elemental metal powders via in-flight alloying. A high-temperature plasma jet ( > 5000 K) is employed for rapid heating/cooling (103 − 105 K s−1), and demonstrates the synthesis of CrFeCoNiMo HEA NPs ( ~ 50 nm) at a high rate approaching 35 g h−1 with a conversion efficiency of 42%. Our thermofluid simulation reveals that the properties of HEA NPs can be tailored by the plasma gas which affects the thermal history of NPs. The HEA NPs demonstrate an excellent light absorption of > 96% over a wide spectrum, representing great potential for photothermal conversion of solar energy at large scales. cited_evidence.text: We carried out control experiments to verify the assumption that the strategy of pyrolysis reduction of mixed metal precursors governed the formation of alloys (Fig. 4). We took the ternary (NiPdPt@GO) alloy as an example to investigate the influence of different pyrolysis strategies on alloy formation, because more elements will make the characterization much more complicated and challenging. In the FMBP process, the NiPdPt alloy was formed without phase segregation (Fig. 4b). In contrast, as shown in Fig. 4d, when the propulsion speed was decreased to 1 cm s−1 (20 s for precursors to reach the heating zone), namely the slow moving bed pyrolysis (SMBP), the phase-separated NiPdPt nanoparticle was clearly formed, where Pt and Pd were not uniformly in the NiPdPt nanoparticles. More obviously, Pd only existed in the core of NiPdPt nanoparticles obtained by the conventional FBP strategy (923 K) with a heating rate of 20 K min−1 (~31 min from 298 K to 923 K), indicating a completely phase segregation (Fig. 4f, Supplementary Fig. 22).
